source.title: UK padel has doubled, but there's subtlety beneath it. | The Court Report
source.text:
The Court Report · August 2026

UK padel has doubled, but there's subtlety beneath it.

In the twelve months to August 2025 the UK approved 312
padel planning applications with 629 lodged. In the twelve months since, it has
approved 649 with 1,150 lodged. Here is what you need to know.

James Morgenstern · 31 August 2026 · 8 minute read · August is provisional

01 — The year to date

The pipeline has doubled

649 Applications approved From 312 +108%

1,150 Applications lodged From 629 +83%

945 Courts approved From 456 +107%

86% Approval rate From 87%. Unchanged.

85 Median decision, days From 84. Unchanged.

2.68 Average scheme, courts From 2.64. Unchanged.

Courts, approvals and applications doubled in the same number of days, at the same
average size. The twelve months to August 2026 include a provisional August, so all
three volume figures are floors.

Submissions and approvals, monthly

Submitted
Approved

Interactive Hover or tap any month for its figures.

UK padel planning applications by month of validation (submitted) and month
of decision (approved), including amendments to consented schemes. August is provisional
and will be locked in by the end of September. Expect it to grow as councils report late.

Growth is still accelerating rather than levelling off. December alone carried 131
applications, the biggest month on record, and every one of the last four quarters has
beaten the same quarter a year earlier.

The quieter movement in that chart is the two bars converging. In March there were 70
approvals against 115 submissions. By July it was 72 against 93. The winter surge is
finally reaching determination, which means a good part of this year's approvals is a
queue clearing rather than fresh demand.

02 — Beneath the numbers

What is actually happening

The volume is the easy part of this story. Five things underneath it change what you
would actually build, and where. Jump straight to any of them.

Scheme size. Every size of scheme grew. The small end just grew four times faster.

The format. Big padel has become a conversion business, not a construction one.

Cover. A roof is the price of scale.

Recent months. August cleared faster than any month bar February, and refused more.

Demand. Supply is now growing faster than play.

03 — Scheme size

The market is tilting small

Approved schemes by court count

Year to Aug 2025
Year to Aug 2026

Interactive Hover or tap a band to compare the two years.

Share of approved new-court schemes where the court count is stated in the
application. n = 173 (to Aug 2025) and 352 (to Aug 2026). Roughly a third of
applications never name a number and are excluded.

Read that chart as a shift in emphasis rather than a decline. Three and four court
schemes went from 71 approvals to 97 , up 37%. They fall from 41% to 28%
of the mix only because the small end grew close to four times faster, from 88 approvals
to 201.

The small end is bolt-ons: two courts added to a tennis club, a cricket club, a school,
a pub car park. The large end is conversions in big sheds, where the maths often favours
economies of scale. The mid-size standalone build, four courts on a piece of land, is
still going up in greater numbers than a year ago. It is simply no longer where the
growth is.

A roof is the price of scale. Covered and indoor schemes average 3.18
courts against 2.51 outdoor, and the covered share of approvals rose from 31% to 38%.
Above four courts, an uncovered UK scheme is close to a rounding error.

Why is less certain from the planning data alone. It may be the cost of canopies and
groundworks, which only starts to make sense spread across more courts. Or it may be that
operators are moving towards an all-in-one venue, with a gym, pilates and other amenities
alongside the courts, and that model needs a big box unit to begin with.

04 — The structural story

Padel is absorbing empty buildings

Change of use went from 22% of new-court submissions in the year to August 2025 to
29% in the year since, and conversions out of industrial, warehouse and
retail stock went from 50 applications to 151.

August's approvals read like a survey of what British high streets and trading estates
have stopped needing: a former Homebase on Finchley Road, a furniture showroom in
Carlisle, the old Floors To Go building in Bury, and the list goes on.

Conversions are not significantly larger on average. But at the top of the market they
are close to the only thing happening.

05 — Last month

July was bigger than we told you

Last month's issue reported 63 applications lodged in July. Now that the portals have
caught up, the confirmed figure is 93 . Approvals moved from 69 to 72,
withdrawals from 11 to 13, refusals from 5 to 7.

Reported on the first of August, July looked like a sharp fall from June. It was not.
July was an ordinary month that had been given one day to be published. We watched it
fill in: 63 on 1 August, 79 by the 20th, 93 today, and it is still not finished.

Because of this we now only confirm a month's figures in the month that follows it.
Here is August so far, provisional, with our projections.

Why August is provisional

On average, councils publish to their planning portals about 16 days late, and some
are much later, so a month keeps filling in after it has ended.

July's numbers are locked. August's are provisional and will rise.

06 — The month

What August put through

August · provisional
Counted to 31 August. Smaller figures are the projected full month.

42 Applications approved 55–65 projected for August
July, confirmed: 72

59 Courts approved ~85 projected for August
July, confirmed: 100

48 Applications lodged ~110 projected for August
July, confirmed: 93

81% Approval rate 42 approved of 52 decided
Twelve-month average: 86%

63 Median decision, days Second fastest in the two-year series
Twelve-month median: 85

Councils cleared August's padel casework faster than any month in the two years we have
tracked bar February, and refused a fifth of it while doing so. Expect that reading to
slip: the back half of the month is only part counted, and the slower cases are the ones
still to arrive.

Do not over-read the refusals. The monthly rate has swung between 7% and 20% since
March, and across the last six months it sits at 14% against 13% for the twelve months
before. Nothing structural has changed.

decision, with filters for court count, application type and decision status.

07 — August in detail

The month's biggest decisions

August's average approved scheme was 3.28 courts, the highest monthly reading in the
series, until you take out Camden and Hertfordshire. Without those two it is 2.50, below
the twelve-month average. August did not produce bigger schemes. It produced two big
ones.

Camden is the one to watch. Ten courts under an all-weather canopy in a
dead Homebase on Finchley Road, on a temporary consent, is the clearest statement yet of
the economics: a covered product that trades all winter, and a lease short enough that
the landlord keeps the redevelopment option. Expect it copied.

Hertfordshire is the one to think about. Nine courts at a sports ground
there were consented retrospectively. They were already built. Retrospective applications
have run at 3 to 6% of submissions all year, which says something quiet about how far
ahead of planning some operators are willing to run.

On the other side, ten refusals, and not marginal ones: one scheme of five courts and
two more of four. Three of the ten were warehouse or industrial conversions, so the shed
route is not sailing through unopposed.

08 — Demand side

Consents are the easy half

The harder question is whether the courts already open are busy. Across the clubs we
track, average occupancy was down in August against July.

Some of that is the calendar. August is the emptiest stretch of the padel year here, and
this one was hot enough that plenty of people who would normally book did not fancy a
game in over 30°. But the denominator moved too: the open fleet keeps adding courts
faster than bookings are growing to fill them, and average court pricing has not moved to
defend it. It is too early to know whether supply is outpacing demand, but it certainly
does not feel like it. We will see what September does.

Besides, occupancy alone can be a poor scoreboard. The two highest revenue-generating
padel clubs in the country in August were Carbon Padel Club and
Rocks Lane Chiswick , and they finished within a whisker of each other
despite being different businesses: Carbon on seventeen courts, Rocks Lane on twelve.
Neither ran the highest occupancy rate in the country. Court count, price and the shape
of the booking day decide the revenue, and counterintuitively, a club optimising for a
full grid can often be leaving money on the table.

Club X-Ray: every bookable club in the country, with occupancy, price and
estimated revenue. Names are blurred here, not in the product.

Try it today.
Open X-Ray →

09 — Where this goes

Three things to watch in September

Whether the convergence holds. If September's approvals come in above
its submissions, the winter backlog is genuinely cleared and the market is running at its
natural rate rather than working through a queue.

Sheds. Conversions have tripled in a year and now carry the top end.
Three of August's ten refusals were conversions. One month is noise, but if that ratio
holds through autumn it constrains the only route currently producing eight-court
venues.

Whether the new courts fill. The consented pipeline is roughly half the
size of the open market, and much of it is covered courts in northern industrial cities
that have never had a padel club. Planning tells you what is coming. Occupancy tells you
whether it should. Next issue we will report occupancy and revenue across the whole of
August and show how the numbers actually moved.
